rv.q: Cromer has taken a mostly prosaic, procedural media drama and turned it into something that scorches with the heat of today's political turmoil.
It packs a wallop — and so does this production.

Irrespective of the strengths and weaknesses of Good Night, and Good Luck as theater, the personal commitment of Clooney, whose father is a former anchorman, seems heartfelt and impassioned. There’s no doubting the sincerity of his belief that this dark chapter of American history has something vital to impart to us in 2025.
The play ends, at least, like a pulse-pounding thriller, emphasizing its through line to the present with a heavy but fiercely effective hand.
With Good Night, and Good Luck, Clooney and his collaborators give a dignified and resonant answer.
And then, the curtain call, to remind you that whatever came before, the actors are fine, drinking in your appreciation and sending you out happy and exhilarated and perhaps full of hope.
The “Glengarry” script is as dynamically notated as a musical score, and it offers little room for interpretation; an actor has to drill deep to make an impression.
But what the staging delivers in newsroom cacophony, it loses in nuance, character and the entrancing mood of momentous defiance.
Good Night, and Good Luck’s message is solid, less so its mode of delivery.

Good Night, and Good Luck is, to my eyes, a sturdy contribution to the sparsely populated landscape of recent political drama.

The original’s focus on the unchecked power of an elected official using fear, rumor, and lies against his enemies obviously hits even harder in 2025... But another theme lightly touched on in the movie — the future role of television in our society — gets even greater emphasis on the stage.
The message is clear: if no one stands up, history isn’t just doomed to repeat—it already is.
The true events depicted in Good Night, and Good Luck not only speak to the McCarthy era but are also relevant to our present divisive time and government.
If there’s not much change in content, “Good Night, and Good Luck” is transformed by its context.

cn.t: Critics praise Clooney's charisma and David Cromer's direction, finding the show timely and well-crafted, but many fault it as a too-faithful film adaptation that feels static and preachy, lacking theatrical vitality despite its urgent message.

sg.ra: With a 44'10" proscenium and a stage wider than most Broadway houses, Orchestra Center C-G is the only zone where you get the full picture head-on without sacrificing actor-face detail. Spectacle-heavy productions here (BTTF's DeLorean, Mamma Mia! dance numbers) are blocked edge-to-edge, so off-center seats lose pieces even a few rows in.

This is the house's quiet value zone: full center alignment matters more here than proximity does because the auditorium is wider than deep, so row V center still reads front-on. Last orchestra row is short (~6 seats) with unusual legroom per multiple patrons. Tradeoff specific to Winter Garden: the mezzanine overhang starts around row O per published guides, clipping the top of the stage — fine for naturalistic plays, worse for musicals with fly-in sets.

Wide-house penalty hits hardest here: because the auditorium is broader than deep, side-orchestra angles into the stage are sharper than in a typical Broadway house — the further out you sit, the more the upstage far corner disappears. Multiple patrons specifically call out stage-right pillars clipping their view on Salesman; works better for plays where action holds center than for musicals with full-stage choreography.

In a wider-than-deep house the front center mezzanine rescues the seat selection by giving you the one thing center orchestra can't: altitude to take in the full 44'10" proscenium at once. Multiple patrons specifically cite this row range for Mamma Mia! and BTTF over the rear orchestra, and it avoids both the pillar risk on the sides and the mezz overhang clipping rear stalls.

Wide-house geometry pushes the far-left and far-right mezz off at a sharp angle — the stage-opposite corner is the consistent casualty. Reviewers note the speaker stacks on the edge as a recurring blocker, and because the mezz is only ~9 rows deep, distance isn't the killer — angle is. Good option if you're watching a show where the action centers; poor for full-stage choreography.

sg.ra: The Winter Garden boxes are widely flagged as among the most obstructed in Broadway — the box structure itself blocks significant stage area and the side angle compounds it. Skip at any price.
